nameStory: The longfin inshore squid gets its name from two key features that make it easy to remember. Unlike many deep-sea squid species, this one lives close to shore in coastal waters where people can actually encounter it. The 'longfin' part refers to the distinctive triangular fins that extend along most of its body, making it look like it's wearing a flowing cape underwater.
description: The longfin inshore squid is a torpedo-shaped marine animal with eight arms, two longer tentacles, and large, intelligent eyes. These agile swimmers have translucent bodies that can quickly change color from pale white to deep reddish-brown, often displaying intricate patterns of spots and stripes. They typically grow to about 6-12 inches long including their tentacles. You'll most likely encounter them washed up on beaches or spot them darting through shallow coastal waters in small groups.

idTips.label: Triangular fins
idTips.description: Long, diamond-shaped fins run along most of the body length, feeling thin and delicate like wet tissue paper when fresh

idTips.label: Color-changing ability
idTips.description: Body can rapidly shift from transparent white to mottled brown with dark spots and wavy lines - even dead specimens may show faint color patterns

idTips.label: Ten appendages
idTips.description: Eight shorter arms with small suction cups you can feel as tiny bumps, plus two longer feeding tentacles with larger sucker pads at the tips

idTips.label: Large prominent eyes
idTips.description: Huge, round black eyes on either side of the head - often the most striking feature and surprisingly human-like in appearance

idTips.label: Torpedo body shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, bullet-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when fresh, with smooth, slightly slimy skin

idTips.label: Internal shell
idTips.description: Contains a clear, flexible internal 'pen' or gladius that feels like a thin piece of plastic if you gently probe the body

habitat: Look for longfin inshore squid in shallow coastal waters from Cape Cod to Long Island Sound, typically in depths of 20-100 feet over sandy or muddy bottoms. They prefer areas with moderate water temperatures and are often found near eelgrass beds where small fish and crustaceans - their preferred prey - are abundant. You're most likely to find them washed up on sandy beaches after storms or spot them in tide pools and shallow bays.

seasonality.spring: Adults move into warmer inshore waters for mating season. Fresh specimens and egg masses may wash up on beaches during spring storms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when squid are most abundant in shallow waters. Best time for beach finds and tide pool discoveries.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue feeding heavily in coastal areas before moving to deeper waters. Still commonly found washed ashore after rough weather.
seasonality.winter: Most squid move to deeper, warmer offshore waters. Beach finds become less common but still possible after major storms.

funFact: Longfin inshore squid can literally rewrite their skin like a living computer screen - they have over a million color-changing cells called chromatophores that can create complex moving patterns faster than you can blink, essentially allowing them to become living mood rings that display their emotions and intentions in real-time.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small cuttlefish or other squid species, but longfin inshore squid are the only squid you're likely to find in New England's shallow coastal waters. If you find a squid-like creature on a New England beach, it's almost certainly this species. Remember: if it has ten arms total and long fins, it's your longfin squid.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their alien appearance, squid are actually mollusks - they're more closely related to clams and snails than to fish. The 'squid' name comes from an old English word meaning 'sea arrow,' referring to their swift, dart-like swimming style.
compareHints: Since this is the only Doryteuthis species in New England waters, compare it to other squid family members you might encounter. Longfin inshore squid are distinguished by their proportionally longer fins and coastal habitat preferences, while deep-sea squid species are typically smaller, have shorter fins, and are rarely found in shallow water. The triangular fin shape extending most of the body length is the key feature that separates this species from other squid.
